egypt_status.national_evidence: A 2022 survey tested maize grain samples from 25 maize-growing governorates in Egypt and detected U. maydis with very high frequency; it was among the fungi detected in 100% of the samples and had high teliospore abundance.
egypt_status.field_survey_evidence: A Minia Governorate survey covering more than 90 villages found symptoms from about 45-day-old plants, with infection increasing to a maximum around 80–90 days.

early_stage: Small pale green or yellowish swellings on young tissues
Localised swelling or distortion at infection sites, especially after wounds or insect damage
characteristic_galls: Round, oval, elongated, or irregular tumour-like galls
Galls may occur on leaves, stalks, nodes, tassels, axillary buds, or ears
Young galls are pale green to silvery-white and covered by a smooth membrane
Galls enlarge rapidly and become greyish-white, silver-grey, or pale brown
Mature galls rupture to expose a dark brown to black mass of powdery teliospores
ear_symptoms: Individual kernels or groups of kernels become greatly swollen galls
Infected ears may be distorted, partially replaced by galls, or poorly filled
Galls on ears are visually prominent and can be much larger than leaf or tassel galls
leaf_and_stalk_symptoms: Small galls may appear on leaf blades or leaf sheaths
Stalk galls can cause local swelling, bending, or weakening
Tassel infection may produce swollen floral tissues and reduced fertility
image_annotation_targets: ruptured gall with black powdery teliospores
ear versus stalk versus tassel infection
distortion and swelling of individual kernels

symptoms: pale green or yellow swollen tissues
gall_surface: black powdery interior after membrane rupture
distribution_on_plant: All above-ground organs can be infected. Ear, stalk, tassel, and apical-meristem galls are the most visually important; young plants may develop galls near growing points.
progression: The pathogen enters susceptible tissues, particularly through wounds or actively growing tissues.
A small swelling develops at the infection site.
The swelling enlarges into a pale, membrane-covered gall.
The gall becomes grey-white or silver-grey and may distort the infected organ.
The membrane ruptures, releasing a dense dark brown or black powder of teliospores.
After spore release, the gall collapses, dries, and leaves a dark, shrivelled mass or scar.

egypt_field_timing.first_observation: Symptoms may be visible from approximately 45 days after planting in Minia field surveys.
egypt_field_timing.maximum_infection_period: The Minia survey reported maximum infection around 80–90 days after planting.
egypt_field_timing.note: Timing varies with cultivar, planting date, tissue susceptibility, injury, and weather.

environment.humidity: Moist conditions and high humidity around infection sites favour spore germination and infection; Egyptian greenhouse inoculation maintained high humidity for 24 hours after inoculation.
environment.temperature: Egyptian pathogenicity work used approximately 30 °C for teliospore germination and 30–35 °C in greenhouse experiments; these are experimental conditions, not a national field optimum.
environment.rain_and_irrigation: Rain, irrigation, and wet plant surfaces support infection, especially when tissues are wounded.
major_risk_factors: hail, wind, insects, or cultivation injuries
mechanical damage to roots, stalks, leaves, or ears
continuous maize and infected crop debris
environment.egypt_weather_context: A 2019 Egyptian maize survey recorded April–August mean temperatures of 25.5–32.9 °C and relative humidity of 18.8–75.2%; U. maydis occurrence and teliospore density varied among governorates.

egypt_isolate_evidence.pathogenicity: Egyptian isolates varied substantially in pathogenicity. The Beni-Suef isolate was most pathogenic in the cited study, while the Kafr El-Sheikh isolate was least pathogenic.
egypt_isolate_evidence.host_response: TWC-Baraka, TWC-322, and SC-129 were among the more resistant tested accessions; Giza-2, Boushi, TWC-320, TWC-324, TWC-321, and DC Dahab were among the more susceptible materials in the cited Egyptian experiments.

yield_impact_evidence_egypt.highest_risk_site: Ear galls caused the greatest yield reductions in Sakha and Gemmeiza experiments.
yield_impact_evidence_egypt.reported_effect: Artificial ear infection was associated with approximately 87–92% grain-yield reduction in the cited field experiments; natural infection was much lower in those trials.
yield_impact_evidence_egypt.caution: These figures are experiment-specific and should not be interpreted as a national average.

similar_diseases.name: Head smut
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Usually replaces or transforms the tassel or ear into a mass of dark spores, often without the large individual membrane-covered galls typical of common smut.

similar_diseases.name: Fusarium ear rot
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Produces pink, white, or reddish mould and kernel rot rather than discrete swollen tumours filled with black teliospores.

similar_diseases.name: Insect or hail injury
similar_diseases.visual_difference: May produce wounds or scars but does not form expanding membrane-covered galls with black powdery spores.

diagnostic_caution: Large swollen galls with a dark powdery teliospore interior are strongly suggestive of common smut. Confirm doubtful samples microscopically or molecularly, especially when ear rot, head smut, insect injury, or other tumour-like symptoms are present.
